channel.title: Brave New Hive
channel.description: A marketing pedia for brands in the age of AI. Every entry dated, sourced and signed by Anne Becheru.

item.title: Brand versus reputation: what is the difference?
item.description: A brand is what a company says and shows about itself. A reputation is what others conclude from what it does. One is authored, the other is earned, and in a buying meeting the second one decides.

item.title: How AI engines answer marketing questions: a citation study
item.description: We asked a live AI engine eight marketing questions and checked every source it named. For six of the eight it never searched, and 21 of the 52 sources it listed do not exist.

item.title: How the AI search vocabulary moved in a year
item.description: Three terms for the same worry, tracked month by month. AI marketing spiked and settled, generative engine optimization drifted down from its peak, and answer engine optimization held flat at a lower level.

item.title: What is AI marketing?
item.description: AI marketing is the use of AI systems in marketing work: to research buyers, generate and test creative, target and bid, and to earn a place in the answers AI assistants give when buyers ask for a recommendation.

item.title: What people search for in marketing: the demand map
item.description: US monthly search volumes for the topics a marketing reference site might cover. The concept names win, the author names do not, and two categories we planned barely exist as searches.

item.title: How Brands Grow. Byron Sharp (2010)
item.description: The evidence-based case that brands grow by reaching more buyers, not by deepening loyalty. Built on decades of purchase data from the Ehrenberg-Bass Institute.

item.title: What is generative engine optimization (GEO)?
item.description: Generative engine optimization, or GEO, is the practice of writing and structuring content so that generative engines cite it in the answers they produce. The term comes from a 2023 research paper by Pranjal Aggarwal and colleagues.

item.title: The Edelman Trust Barometer
item.description: An annual survey of trust in business, government, media and NGOs, published by Edelman every year since 2001. It is the most cited public measure of institutional trust.

item.title: Ogilvy on Advertising. David Ogilvy (1983)
item.description: The working manual of the man who built Ogilvy & Mather, on headlines, layouts, research and the difference between advertising that wins awards and advertising that sells.

item.title: What is answer engine optimization (AEO)?
item.description: Answer engine optimization, or AEO, is the practice of preparing content so that it is used in a direct answer rather than a list of links. In practice it means answering one question per page, plainly and early.

item.title: 1982. The Tylenol case
item.description: After seven people in the Chicago area died from cyanide-laced Tylenol capsules, Johnson & Johnson recalled the product nationwide and introduced tamper-evident packaging. It remains the reference case in crisis communications.

item.title: What is AI SEO?
item.description: AI SEO means two things: using AI tools to do SEO work faster, and optimising a site so that AI search features and assistants surface it. The second is the one that decides whether a brand appears in an answer.

item.title: Positioning: The Battle for Your Mind. Al Ries and Jack Trout (1981)
item.description: The book that moved the battleground from the product to the prospect's mind. Own a word, or a place relative to the leader, before someone else does.

item.title: The 4 Ps of marketing
item.description: The marketing mix says a marketer's job is to set four controllable variables: product, price, place and promotion. It is a classification, not a theory, and has never been tested as one.

item.title: What is trust architecture?
item.description: Trust architecture is the deliberate arrangement of proof around a company so that a buyer, a journalist or a model can verify its claims without asking. At Brave New it is the name of that discipline.

item.title: What is a retrievable brand?
item.description: A retrievable brand is one that AI assistants and search engines can find, name and describe correctly when a buyer asks. It is built from clear definitions, named frameworks, sourced facts and one consistent description repeated everywhere.

item.title: 1841. Who invented the advertising agency
item.description: Volney Palmer opened the first US ad agency in 1841, paid by the newspapers. How that commission shaped agencies to the Mad Men era, and what replaced it.

item.title: Thinking, Fast and Slow. Daniel Kahneman (2011)
item.description: Kahneman's summary of forty years of research with Amos Tversky on how judgement works in practice: two systems, one fast and automatic, one slow and lazy.

item.title: How do AI models choose which brands to recommend?
item.description: Models answer from what they were trained on and what they can retrieve at the moment of the question. A brand gets named when it is described the same way across many independent sources and is easy to quote.

item.title: What is reputation risk?
item.description: Reputation risk is the chance that an event, a decision or a disclosure changes what stakeholders believe about a company, and with it the company's ability to sell, hire, borrow or be regulated on the same terms.

item.title: The Coke and Pepsi brain study (the Pepsi paradox)
item.description: McClure and colleagues, Neuron, 2004. Told which cola they were drinking, people's stated preference and their brain activity both changed. The brand did the work the taste did not.

item.title: This Note's for You. Neil Young (1988)
item.description: A refusal to sell songs to sponsors, with a title that parodies a beer slogan. MTV initially declined to air the video, then gave it Video of the Year in 1989.

item.title: Positioning in marketing
item.description: Positioning, as Ries and Trout set it out in 1972, claims that a brand wins by occupying one clear slot in the prospect's memory. The memory half holds up.

item.title: Thank You for Smoking (2005)
item.description: Jason Reitman's satire follows a tobacco lobbyist who can argue any side. A film about spin, and about the difference between persuasion and truth.

item.title: The Long and the Short of It. Les Binet and Peter Field (2013)
item.description: The IPA study of what produced measurable business effects across hundreds of campaigns: brand building and sales activation work on different timescales and need different creative.

item.title: How do I get my company mentioned in ChatGPT and Perplexity answers?
item.description: Publish a plain definition of what you do, keep that description identical everywhere it appears, earn coverage on the sources the engines already cite, and make your pages easy to read, date and attribute. Then check the answers monthly.

item.title: 1922. The first paid radio commercial
item.description: On 28 August 1922 a property firm paid WEAF $50 to talk about apartments. What radio's first thirty years say about sponsoring a show versus buying the spot.

item.title: Alchemy. Rory Sutherland (2019)
item.description: Sutherland's argument that the most valuable ideas in business do not survive a spreadsheet, because people do not choose the way economics assumes they do.

item.title: What is llms.txt?
item.description: llms.txt is a plain text file placed at the root of a website that gives AI systems a short, curated summary of the site and links to its most useful pages. Jeremy Howard of Answer.AI proposed it in 2024.

item.title: Sell Out. Reel Big Fish (1996)
item.description: A ska-punk band signs to a major label and writes a hit about signing to a major label. The commercial bargain, sung from inside it.

item.title: System 1 and System 2 thinking in marketing
item.description: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow, 2011. Most decisions, including most purchases, run on the fast, automatic system, and the slow one mostly rationalises afterwards.

item.title: Influence. Robert Cialdini (1984)
item.description: Cialdini's six principles of persuasion, reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity, each traced to the research and the compliance professionals who use it.

item.title: Market segmentation
item.description: Market segmentation claims a market is not one demand curve but several, and that a firm does better serving some of them well than all of them adequately. The evidence supports that claim for categories: buyers differ in what they want and how much they use.

item.title: The Founder (2016)
item.description: Ray Kroc turns a single hamburger stand into McDonald's. The product was the brothers'. The brand, the system and the name became his.

item.title: Why does brand consistency matter for AI search?
item.description: Because a model reads every version of your company that exists online and averages them. Three different descriptions produce a vague answer or no answer. One description, repeated exactly, produces a sentence the model can quote.

item.title: 1941. The first television commercial
item.description: The $9 Bulova spot of 1 July 1941 created the paid TV unit. Why it took thirty years, a scandal and a tobacco ban to become the 30-second spot you buy today.

item.title: Art & Copy (2009)
item.description: Doug Pray's documentary on the creative revolution in advertising, with Lee Clow, George Lois, Mary Wells Lawrence, Hal Riney and others on the work that defined the trade.

item.title: Television, the Drug of the Nation. The Disposable Heroes of Hiphoprisy (1992)
item.description: Michael Franti's spoken-word indictment of broadcast media, consumption and attention, written before the feed replaced the channel.

item.title: Unique selling proposition (USP)
item.description: Rosser Reeves set out the unique selling proposition in 1961 as a three-part rule: every advertisement must offer a specific benefit, competitors must not claim it, and it must be strong enough to pull new buyers. His evidence was agency data.

item.title: The somatic marker hypothesis
item.description: Antonio Damasio, Descartes' Error, 1994. Emotion is part of the machinery of choosing, not noise laid over reason. Patients who lost it could not decide.

item.title: 1960. The 4 Ps of marketing are published
item.description: 1960: McCarthy's four Ps and Levitt's Marketing Myopia turned marketing into a taught discipline, and left the agency holding one box out of four.

item.title: Mental availability and physical availability
item.description: Sharp's claim is that brands grow by being easy to think of and easy to buy, because loyalty follows market share rather than causing it. The second half is well tested: double jeopardy holds in 32 differentiated replications, in cars, business banking, aircraft and packaged goods.

item.title: The Greatest Movie Ever Sold (2011)
item.description: Morgan Spurlock makes a documentary about product placement, funded entirely by product placement. The pitch meetings are the film.

item.title: Money. Pink Floyd (1973)
item.description: Cash registers as percussion, a 7/4 riff, and a lyric about the economy of wanting. From The Dark Side of the Moon.

item.title: Where the word came from
item.description: The term neuromarketing is commonly credited to Ale Smidts of Erasmus University in Rotterdam, in 2002.

item.title: 1972. The Positioning Era Cometh
item.description: In April 1972 Ries and Trout told Advertising Age the battleground had moved to the prospect's mind. What Avis, Volkswagen and 7-Up had proved, and what to do now.

item.title: The Long and the Short of It
item.description: Binet and Field claim that advertising works in two modes on two clocks: activation sells now and fades, brand building sells later and compounds, so budgets should lean long, at roughly 60:40. The evidence is 996 award entries in which volume arrives within months, pricing power takes years, and efficiency peaks at 30 to 50 percent activation.

item.title: The Century of the Self (2002)
item.description: Adam Curtis's four-part BBC series on Edward Bernays and how ideas from psychoanalysis were used to shape public relations, advertising and consumer culture.

item.title: Material Girl. Madonna (1984)
item.description: Consumer desire as identity, delivered as pop. The video restages Marilyn Monroe's Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend.

item.title: Processing fluency in marketing
item.description: Things that are easy to read, see and say are judged more true and more likeable. Reber, Schwarz and Winkielman set the effect out in 2004.

item.title: 1994. The first banner ad
item.description: HotWired ran the first banners on 27 October 1994. What the 44 per cent click rate and the fall to 0.1 per cent mean for your display budget.

item.title: AIDA
item.description: AIDA claims that a buyer passes through attention, interest, desire and action in that order, and that a message should push them along it. The attribution to E. St. Elmo Lewis in 1898 rests on one uncited sentence in a 1925 textbook; the four steps first appear in salesmanship magazines of 1903 and 1904 under other names.

item.title: How to Get Ahead in Advertising (1989)
item.description: Bruce Robinson's comedy about an ad executive whose crisis of conscience grows into a talking boil that wants his job.

item.title: Loss aversion in marketing
item.description: Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory, 1979. Losses weigh roughly twice as much as gains of the same size. Most urgency in marketing borrows from this.

item.title: 2000. Google launches AdWords
item.description: In October 2000 Google let any business buy a search query. The AdWords record, the auction, the commission it bypassed, and what to do with it.

item.title: Advertising Space. Robbie Williams (2005)
item.description: A ballad about Elvis Presley and what fame does to a person once the image becomes inventory.

item.title: Brand equity
item.description: Brand equity is the claim that a name adds value beyond what the product does, and that this value can be built, measured and banked. Aaker (1991) listed the assets; Keller (1993) located them in the customer's memory.

item.title: The Joneses (2009)
item.description: A perfect family moves into a wealthy suburb. They are not a family. They are a stealth marketing unit, and everything they own is for sale.

item.title: 2022. ChatGPT is released
item.description: ChatGPT, 30 November 2022: the day the answer replaced the results page. What the record shows, what it changed for brands, and what to do on Monday.

item.title: Don't Believe the Hype. Public Enemy (1988)
item.description: A song about manufactured media narratives and who gets to write them. From It Takes a Nation of Millions to Hold Us Back.

item.title: Mad Men (2007 to 2015)
item.description: Seven seasons of Madison Avenue in the 1960s. The Carousel pitch in the first season is still the best short explanation of what a brand sells.

item.title: Radio Radio. Elvis Costello and the Attractions (1978)
item.description: A protest against commercial radio and the control of what gets heard. Costello famously switched to it mid-performance on Saturday Night Live in 1977.

item.title: Putney Swope (1969)
item.description: Robert Downey Sr.'s satire: the token Black executive at a Madison Avenue agency is accidentally elected chairman and turns the place upside down.
